TRADEMARK OPPOSITION AND CANCELLATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · Beta Corp.

STATEMENT OF THE PROCEEDING AND ITS GROUNDS
This information sheet concerns a opposition before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, brought by Acme, Inc.

The application or registration at issue is identified as: ACME (word mark), used or intended for use on or in connection with: consumer electronics, U.S. application or registration number: Serial No. 90/123,456, standing in the name of Beta Corp.

Acme, Inc. believes it is or would be damaged by this application or registration, and identifies the following as the grounds on which this opposition is based: likelihood of confusion with a prior mark

This statement reflects Acme, Inc.'s current understanding. It is not a decision of the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, and nothing in this statement states that the Board has determined that any ground for opposition or cancellation has been established.

OPPOSITION TO REGISTRATION: WHO MAY OPPOSE, AND THE STATUTORY DEADLINE
Federal trademark law allows any person who believes that he would be damaged by the registration of a mark on the principal register — including damage from a likelihood of dilution by blurring or tarnishment — to file an opposition in the Patent and Trademark Office, upon payment of the prescribed fee and stating the grounds for the opposition. The statute sets a firm deadline for doing so: an opposition must be filed within thirty days after the mark sought to be registered is published for opposition. That thirty-day period is not absolute, however. Upon written request made before the initial thirty-day period expires, the statute extends the time for filing an additional thirty days, and it allows the Director to grant further extensions for good cause when requested before an already-granted extension expires. An opposition proceeding exists only against a mark that has been published but not yet registered; once the opposition period passes without a successful opposition, the statute directs that the mark proceed either to registration or, for an intent-to-use application, to a notice of allowance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who believes that he would be damaged by the registration of a mark upon the principal register, including the registration of any mark which would be likely to cause dilution by blurring or dilution by tarnishment under section 1125(c) of this title , may, upon payment of the prescribed fee, file an opposition in the Patent and Trademark Office, stating the grounds therefor, within thirty days after the publication under subsection (a) of section 1062 of this title of the mark sought to be registered."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1063(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, opposition to registration — who may oppose and the thirty-day deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1063)
  "Upon written request prior to the expiration of the thirty-day period, the time for filing opposition shall be extended for an additional thirty days, and further extensions of time for filing opposition may be granted by the Director for good cause when requested prior to the expiration of an extension."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1063(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, extension of the opposition deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1063)
  Known gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide), used as real evidence of the statutory opposition deadline and who may invoke it — not a claim that any opposition to the mark described on this sheet has been or should be filed, which this clause does not resolve. This clause quotes a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1063(a)); its two citations are both drawn from that one subsection and are not independent sources of each other. The statute's text itself does not enumerate which substantive grounds an opposition may assert — it requires only that the opposition state its grounds; see the companion clause on grounds common to both opposition and cancellation proceedings. This research pass found uspto.gov unreachable from this session (a direct request returned a blocked connection), so this clause is built on the statutory text itself rather than on the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board's own procedural rules (for example, the specific mechanics of requesting or opposing an extension), which this clause does not describe. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

CANCELLATION OF A REGISTERED MARK: WHO MAY PETITION, AND HOW THE AVAILABLE GROUNDS NARROW OVER TIME
Federal trademark law allows a petition to cancel a registration, stating the grounds relied upon, to be filed upon payment of the prescribed fee by any person who believes that he is or will be damaged by the registration of a mark on the principal register — including damage from a likelihood of dilution. The statute then sets the timing for that petition in two structurally different ways. First, a petition may be filed within five years from the date of registration, without that time-limited provision itself restricting, in its own text, which grounds may be raised during that window. Second, and separately, the statute lists specific grounds that may instead be asserted at any time — meaning without regard to whether the five-year period above has already run — including that the registered mark has become the generic name for the goods or services (or a portion of them) for which it is registered, that it has become functional, that it has been abandoned, or that its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to certain other statutory provisions. Because those specific grounds are the ones the statute frees from the five-year time limit, a registration that has stood for more than five years can still be challenged, but the challenge must fit within one of those enumerated "at any time" grounds rather than being filed as an otherwise-unrestricted five-year-window petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A petition to cancel a registration of a mark, stating the grounds relied upon, may, upon payment of the prescribed fee, be filed as follows by any person who believes that he is or will be damaged, including as a result of a likelihood of dilution by blurring or dilution by tarnishment under section 1125(c) of this title , by the registration of a mark on the principal register established by this chapter, or under the Act of March 3, 1881 , or the Act of February 20, 1905 :"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1064 (introductory clause) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, who may petition to cancel a registered mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1064)
  "Within five years from the date of the registration of the mark under this chapter."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1064(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the general five-year window to petition for cancellation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1064)
  "At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to the provisions of section 1054 of this title or of subsection (a), (b), or (c) of section 1052 of this title for a registration under this chapter, or contrary to similar prohibitory provisions of such prior Acts for a registration under such Acts, or if the registered mark is being used by, or with the permission of, the registrant so as to misrepresent the source of the goods or services on or in connection with which the mark is used."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, grounds for cancellation available at any time (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1064)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the cancellation standing requirement and the statute's two-track timing structure — not a claim that any registration described on this sheet is or is not subject to cancellation on any particular ground or within any particular window, which this clause does not resolve. This clause's three citations are all drawn from the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1064, its introductory clause and paragraphs (1) and (3)); they are not independent of each other. The statute also lists additional "at any time" grounds this clause does not quote in full — including issues specific to a mark registered under superseded 1881 or 1905 Acts, grounds specific to certification marks, and a mark that has never been used in commerce within three years after registration — and a separate, narrower ground already addressed elsewhere in this corpus (abandonment through inadequate licensing control, see the trademark-license document's cancellation-ground clause) is one instance of the "abandoned" ground quoted here, not a duplicate treatment of it. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

STATUTORY GROUNDS THAT MAY SUPPORT AN OPPOSITION OR A CANCELLATION
Two different statutory provisions supply the substantive grounds that can support either type of Trademark Trial and Appeal Board proceeding. The cancellation statute itself names several grounds that are available against a registration at any time: that the registered mark has become the generic name for the goods or services for which it is registered, that it has become functional, that it has been abandoned, or that its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to section 1054 or subsection (a), (b), or (c) of section 1052 of the same title (which bar registration of immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter; certain flags and insignia; and certain names, portraits, or signatures of living individuals, respectively). Separately, the statute governing which marks are registrable in the first place bars registration of a mark that so resembles a mark already registered, or a mark or trade name already used in the United States and not abandoned, that it is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception, and separately bars registration of a mark that is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of the goods on which it is used (subject to the same statute's separate allowance for a mark that has become distinctive through substantially exclusive and continuous use). Confusing similarity and mere descriptiveness are not among the grounds the cancellation statute frees from its five-year time limit; an opposition, by contrast, is filed before registration ever issues and is not subject to that five-year framework at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to the provisions of section 1054 of this title or of subsection (a), (b), or (c) of section 1052 of this title for a registration under this chapter, or contrary to similar prohibitory provisions of such prior Acts for a registration under such Acts"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, grounds for cancellation available at any time (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1064)
  "Consists of or comprises a mark which so resembles a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, or a mark or trade name previously used in the United States by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods of the applicant, to cause confusion, or to cause mistake, or to deceive"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1052(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, bar on registration for likelihood of confusion with an existing mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1052)
  "Consists of a mark which (1) when used on or in connection with the goods of the applicant is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of them,"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1052(e)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, bar on registration for a merely descriptive mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1052)

These are two genuinely independent statutory sections, not subsections of one provision. Note on inference, stated honestly: the opposition statute (15 U.S.C. § 1063(a)) requires only that an opposition "state the grounds therefor" without itself naming which grounds qualify; this clause's statement that confusing similarity and descriptiveness are available in an opposition rests on the registrability statute (§ 1052) defining what disqualifies a mark from registration in the first place, not on § 1063's text naming those grounds explicitly — that connection is well-established Board practice, but this research pass did not verify it against a case or a Board rule (uspto.gov was unreachable this session), so it is disclosed here rather than presented as an explicit statutory statement. This clause does not restate the cancellation statute's other "at any time" grounds not concerning confusion or descriptiveness (certification-mark misuse, nonuse, and marks under superseded acts) — see the companion clause on cancellation timing. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

THE TRADEMARK TRIAL AND APPEAL BOARD'S AUTHORITY IS LIMITED TO THE RIGHT TO REGISTER
Federal trademark law establishes the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board as the body directed to determine and decide the respective rights of registration in every case of opposition, cancellation, interference, or an application to register as a lawful concurrent user; the Director gives notice to the parties and directs the Board to hear the case. The statute then enumerates what the Board (acting through the Director) may do in deciding such a proceeding: refuse to register the opposed mark, cancel a registration in whole or in part, modify an application or registration by limiting the goods or services it covers, otherwise restrict or rectify the register, refuse to register interfering marks, or register the mark for the party entitled to it. That enumerated list of available actions is limited to the register itself; it does not include an award of money damages or an injunction against anyone's use of a mark. Those latter remedies are instead granted, under separate statutory provisions, to "the several courts vested with jurisdiction of civil actions" arising under the same title — a power given to courts hearing civil actions, not to the Board.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In every case of interference, opposition to registration, application to register as a lawful concurrent user, or application to cancel the registration of a mark, the Director shall give notice to all parties and shall direct a Trademark Trial and Appeal Board to determine and decide the respective rights of registration."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1067(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, institution of Board proceedings to determine rights of registration (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1067)
  "In such proceedings the Director may refuse to register the opposed mark, may cancel the registration, in whole or in part, may modify the application or registration by limiting the goods or services specified therein, may otherwise restrict or rectify with respect to the register the registration of a registered mark, may refuse to register any or all of several interfering marks, or may register the mark or marks for the person or persons entitled thereto, as the rights of the parties under this chapter may be established in the proceedings."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1068 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, actions available in an opposition, cancellation, or interference proceeding (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1068)
  "The several courts vested with jurisdiction of civil actions arising under this chapter shall have power to grant injunctions, according to the principles of equity and upon such terms as the court may deem reasonable, to prevent the violation of any right of the registrant of a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1116(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, injunctive relief granted to courts in a civil action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1116)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a structural distinction the statute itself draws between the Board's registration-focused authority and a court's authority in a civil action — not a claim about how any particular dispute involving the mark described on this sheet would or should be brought, which this clause does not address. This clause draws on three independent statutory sections: 15 U.S.C. § 1067(a) (establishing the Board and its charge), § 1068 (the enumerated list of actions available in a Board proceeding), and § 1116(a) (injunctive relief, granted to courts). This clause infers the damages/injunction distinction from what § 1068's enumerated list does and does not include, rather than from a single sentence stating the limitation directly; the same inference is reinforced by 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a), which likewise conditions a damages recovery on a violation "established in any civil action," though that fourth citation is not separately quoted here to avoid restating the same point three times. Part 2, Subpart D) or on case law describing this distinction, neither of which is cited here. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

ABANDONMENT AS A GROUND IN A BOARD PROCEEDING: THE STATUTORY DEFINITION AND THE NONUSE PRESUMPTION
Abandonment is one of the grounds the cancellation statute makes available against a registration at any time, without regard to the general five-year filing window. The statute separately defines what "abandoned" means. One of the two statutory ways a mark is deemed abandoned is when its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume that use; the statute allows that intent to be inferred from the surrounding circumstances, and it sets a specific evidentiary rule: nonuse of a mark for three consecutive years is prima facie evidence of abandonment. The statute also defines "use" for this purpose as bona fide use made in the ordinary course of trade, not use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. Prima facie evidence under this provision shifts the practical burden to the registrant to come forward with evidence of an intent to resume use or otherwise rebut the presumption; it is a presumption arising from a fixed period of nonuse, not itself a finding that abandonment has occurred.

  "When its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume such use . Intent not to resume may be inferred from circumstances. Nonuse for 3 consecutive years shall be prima facie evidence of abandonment."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of "abandoned" — nonuse with intent not to resume, and the three-year presumption (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127)

This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURE
Acme, Inc. certifies that, to the best of its knowledge, information, and belief formed after reasonable inquiry, the statements above are accurate. Nothing in this document is a complete statement of the facts, claims, or legal theories available to Acme, Inc. in connection with this proceeding, and nothing in it waives or limits any right Acme, Inc. may have, all of which are expressly reserved.

Filing a notice of opposition or a petition to cancel with the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board is a formal step in an administrative proceeding heard by the Board rather than by a court. This document does not itself constitute that filing, and completing this information sheet does not itself commence or take any action in a Board proceeding.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, injunctive relief granted to courts in a civil action
citations.quote: The several courts vested with jurisdiction of civil actions arising under this chapter shall have power to grant injunctions, according to the principles of equity and upon such terms as the court may deem reasonable, to prevent the violation of any right of the registrant of a mark registered in the Patent and Trademark Office

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a structural distinction the statute itself draws between the Board's registration-focused authority and a court's authority in a civil action — not a claim about how any particular dispute involving the mark described on this sheet would or should be brought, which this clause does not address. This clause draws on three independent statutory sections: 15 U.S.C. § 1067(a) (establishing the Board and its charge), § 1068 (the enumerated list of actions available in a Board proceeding), and § 1116(a) (injunctive relief, granted to courts). This clause infers the damages/injunction distinction from what § 1068's enumerated list does and does not include, rather than from a single sentence stating the limitation directly; the same inference is reinforced by 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a), which likewise conditions a damages recovery on a violation "established in any civil action," though that fourth citation is not separately quoted here to avoid restating the same point three times. expectedJSON.body: Abandonment is one of the grounds the cancellation statute makes available against a registration at any time, without regard to the general five-year filing window. The statute separately defines what "abandoned" means. One of the two statutory ways a mark is deemed abandoned is when its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume that use; the statute allows that intent to be inferred from the surrounding circumstances, and it sets a specific evidentiary rule: nonuse of a mark for three consecutive years is prima facie evidence of abandonment. The statute also defines "use" for this purpose as bona fide use made in the ordinary course of trade, not use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. Prima facie evidence under this provision shifts the practical burden to the registrant to come forward with evidence of an intent to resume use or otherwise rebut the presumption; it is a presumption arising from a fixed period of nonuse, not itself a finding that abandonment has occurred.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, abandonment as a cancellation ground available at any time
citations.quote: At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently

citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "abandoned" — nonuse with intent not to resume, and the three-year presumption
citations.quote: When its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume such use . Intent not to resume may be inferred from circumstances. Nonuse for 3 consecutive years shall be prima facie evidence of abandonment.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory abandonment definition and its three-year nonuse presumption — not a claim that any mark described on this sheet has or has not been abandoned, which depends on facts about actual use this clause does not evaluate. This clause treats a different statutory basis than the two abandonment-related clauses already in this corpus: the trademark-license document's cancellation-ground clause cites this same cancellation provision (15 U.S.C. § 1064(3)) for the general point that abandonment is a no-time-limit cancellation ground, and its naked-licensing clause cites the definition's second prong (15 U.S.C. § 1127(2), loss of significance through the owner's course of conduct); this clause instead verifies, independently and for the first time in this corpus, the definition's first prong (15 U.S.C. § 1127(1)) — the nonuse-with-intent-not-to-resume definition and its three-year prima facie presumption — as the ground most likely to be at issue specifically in a Board opposition or cancellation proceeding built around nonuse. This clause's two citations are to two independent statutory sections (§ 1064(3) and § 1127(1)), not subsections of the same provision.
